faqs.a: Open DevTools (F12), go to the Network tab, reproduce the page load, then right-click any request and choose Save all as HAR with content (Chrome/Edge) or Save All As HAR (Firefox). Then open or paste the file here.
faqs.q: How do I get a HAR file?

faqs.a: HAR = HTTP Archive. It's a JSON format that records everything the browser did on the network: requests, responses, timings, sizes. Browsers can export it from their Network panels.

Blocked = queuing/proxy time before the request starts. DNS = resolving the hostname. Connect = TCP handshake. SSL = TLS handshake. Send = uploading the request. Wait = server processing (TTFB). Receive = downloading the response. Gray/amber segments at the left usually mean connection overhead; long blue (wait) means a slow server.
faqs.q: What do the waterfall phases mean?

faqs.a: Open the file, paste it here, and look at the totals and the waterfall. Big total bytes means too much transferred; long total time with short waits means many sequential requests — consider bundling or preloading.
faqs.q: How do I find why a page is slow?

faqs.a: You can, but be careful: HAR files can contain cookies, auth tokens, and personal URLs. This viewer processes everything locally and never uploads, so it's the safest way to inspect one. Avoid sending HAR files to strangers or pasting them into random websites.
faqs.q: Is it safe to share a HAR file?

faqs.a: Chrome, Edge, Firefox, and Safari can all export HAR. The format version matters little here — the viewer reads the standard log.entries structure with request, response, and timings.

har-file-viewer.formula:
How the viewer computes things:
- Requests: count of log.entries.
- Size per entry: response.bodySize (or content.size when bodySize is -1).
- Total bytes: sum of sizes ÷ 1024 = KB.
- Total time: (max startedDateTime + time) − (min startedDateTime), in ms.
- Waterfall position: each entry's bar starts at (started − min) ÷ span × 100% and is time ÷ span × 100% wide.
- Phases (blocked, dns, connect, ssl, send, wait, receive) are stacked inside each bar; -1 or 0 values are hidden.
howTo: Export a HAR file from your browser's Network panel (right-click → Save as HAR).
Open the .har file here, or paste its JSON into the box.
Read the totals: requests, transferred KB, and total time.
Study the waterfall: long bars and big blue wait segments are your suspects.
Click through phases in the legend to learn what each colored segment means.
keyFacts: HAR (HTTP Archive) is the standard JSON format for recording browser network activity.
Every request carries per-phase timings: blocked, DNS, connect, SSL, send, wait, receive.
The waterfall turns raw timings into a visual timeline of what loaded when.
Status badges make failures (4xx/5xx) and redirects (3xx) visible at a glance.
HAR files may contain cookies and tokens — inspect them in a local viewer like this one.
Browsers can export HAR directly from the Network tab; no extensions needed.

har-file-viewer.workedExample:
A 2-entry HAR: entry 1 GET https://example.com/ (200, text/html, bodySize 1500, timings blocked 5, dns 10, connect 15, ssl 20, send 2, wait 60, receive 8, time 120, started at T+0) and entry 2 GET https://example.com/style.css (200, text/css, bodySize 800, timings blocked 2, dns 0, connect 0, ssl 0, send 1, wait 50, receive 7, time 60, started at T+100).
Traced by the tool:
1. Requests: 2.
2. Total bytes: 1500 + 800 = 2300 = 2.2 KB.
3. Total time: min start T+0, max end T+100 + 60 = T+160 — 160 ms.
4. Slowest: GET / at 120 ms.
5. Waterfall: bar 1 spans 0%–75% of the track (120/160), bar 2 starts at 62.5% (100/160) and spans to 100%; inside each bar the phases stack left to right (5+10+15+20+2+60+8 = 120 for entry 1 — exactly its time).
